Feuerbach Incidence

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move a triangle and watch how its touching circles line up.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, circles and the two patterns.
Look for the math

Move one corner of the triangle. The circles change shape, but the special points they produce still fall into the same two patterns. That is the incidence in Feuerbach's theorem: points that look unrelated keep meeting or lining up.

Four circles that touch

The nine-point circle passes through the midpoints of the three sides. Feuerbach's theorem says it touches the incircle from the outside of the gap between them, and each excircle from the other side. With circumradius R, inradius r and exradius ra, the centre distances are |NI| = R/2 − r and |NIa| = R/2 + ra. The marks Fa, Fb, Fc and Fi are those four touch points; N is the centre of the nine-point circle, not a touch point, despite the original page calling N "the Feuerbach point".

The concurrence

The lines AFa, BFb and CFc meet in one point F. This point is X(12) in Kimberling's Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers. In side lengths a = BC, b = CA, c = AB, its barycentric coordinates are (b+c)²/(b+c−a) : (c+a)²/(c+a−b) : (a+b)²/(a+b−c). The logic test compares the drawn point with that formula over 500 triangles: they agree to floating-point precision, and all three lines pass through it.

The line through four points

The page's second claim is that N, F, I and Fi lie on one line, called L(1, 5) after the centers X(1) and X(5). Here Fi is the true Feuerbach point X(11). F is the harmonic conjugate of Fi with respect to I and N, which forces all four points to be collinear. The original page says the four points are "concurrent"; for points that means collinear. Both incidences hold in all 500 tested triangles.

How the applet builds them, and its neighbours

The applet finds each centre from two angle bisectors, averages its three distances to the sides for a radius, and puts each touch point on the line of the two centres. This page follows that construction. The checkbox gating is the applet's too: concurrence and collinearity stay switched off until circles are on. A flat or equilateral triangle has no unique touch point, so this port leaves the drawing alone there. The sibling applets ask different questions: Feuerbach states the tangency, FeuerbachProof proves it by inversion, and FeuerbachTreasure counts the tangencies of four triangles sharing one nine-point circle. This applet is the incidence follow-up, and the live cut-the-knot page still embeds it.

Tick all three Show boxes, then drag A close to the side BC. Watch F slide along the line through N, I and Fi.
